question_text: “Constitutionally guaranteed judicial independence is a prerequisite of democracy.” Comment.
topic: Judicial independence as a condition of democracy
topics: Judicial independence as a condition of democracy
keyPointers: A democracy needs a court that can say no to the government of the day
The guarantee is appointment, tenure, salary and a contempt power used with restraint
Independence is from the executive, not from the Constitution or from reason
A court that is only independent, and not accountable, is a different danger

points.text: Democracy is the right of the citizen to have a dispute with the state decided by someone the state does not own.
Security of tenure, a fixed salary charged on the consolidated fund, a difficult removal and the separation of the judiciary are how the Constitution buys that independence.
Without it, an election is only a change of who appoints the judge. Rights, federal disputes and the election itself become political favours.
Independence is a prerequisite. It is not a licence. A democracy also needs a court that explains itself.

question_text: Who are entitled to receive free legal aid? Assess the role of the National Legal Services Authority (NALSA) in rendering free legal aid in India.
topic: Free legal aid and NALSA
topics: Free legal aid and NALSA
keyPointers: The entitlement is of the person who cannot pay, not of every litigant
Article 39A and the Legal Services Authorities Act name the duty
NALSA builds the machinery: lok adalat, clinic and a panel lawyer
The gap is quality and the fact that many entitled people never hear of it

points.text: Free legal aid is a right of those who would otherwise meet the court without a lawyer.
Women, children, Scheduled Castes and Tribes, industrial workmen, persons in custody, and anyone below the income ceiling are among those entitled.
NALSA, with the state and district authorities, runs lok adalats, legal literacy and the assignment of a lawyer at public cost.
The role is real and uneven. Entitlement on paper still fails when the lawyer is absent or the accused does not know the right exists.

question_text: “The states in India seem reluctant to empower urban local bodies both functionally as well as financially.” Comment.
topic: Why states hesitate to empower urban local bodies
topics: Why states hesitate to empower urban local bodies
keyPointers: The 74th Amendment transferred subjects and left the money behind
States keep functions because cities are politically valuable
A body without tax and staff is a local body only in name
Reluctance is fiscal and political at once

points.text: Urban local bodies were constitutionalised and then left dependent on the state that was supposed to let go.
Many functions in the Twelfth Schedule stay with the state department. The city implements a scheme it did not design.
Own taxes are thin, transfers are late, and a parastatal or a development authority holds the land and the water.
The reluctance is rational for a state that wants the city vote and the city land. It is a failure of the 74th Amendment's purpose.

question_text: Compare and contrast the British and Indian approaches to Parliamentary sovereignty.
topic: Parliamentary sovereignty in Britain and India
topics: Parliamentary sovereignty in Britain and India
keyPointers: Britain treats Parliament as legally unlimited
India treats Parliament as supreme inside a written Constitution
Basic structure is the Indian limit Britain does not have
Both trust a parliament; only one lets a court stop it

points.text: Britain's Parliament can make or unmake any law. India's Parliament cannot.
The British approach has no written higher law. A later statute simply overrides an earlier one, and no court strikes an Act down for content.
India gives Parliament wide power, including amendment, and then binds it to the Constitution and to the basic structure a court will enforce.
The contrast is not that India distrusts its Parliament. It is that India wrote down the limits Britain left to convention.

question_text: Discuss the role of Presiding Officers of state legislatures in maintaining order and impartiality in conducting legislative work and in facilitating best democratic practices.
topic: Presiding officers of state legislatures
topics: Presiding officers of state legislatures
keyPointers: The chair is the referee of a house that would otherwise be a party
Order is rulings, discipline and a fair list of business
Impartiality is the part most often doubted
Democratic practice fails when the chair is only the majority's officer

points.text: A state legislature works only if someone who is not the government of the day controls the floor.
The Speaker or Chairman admits questions and motions, applies the rules, and can name a member who will not let the house function.
Impartiality asks the chair to give time to the opposition and to resign party loyalty in the running of the house. That expectation is often missed.
Best practice is a chair who is dull, predictable and unwilling to be useful to the treasury bench.

question_text: The crucial aspect of development process has been the inadequate attention paid to Human Resource Development in India. Suggest measures that can address this inadequacy.
topic: Human resource development as a missing priority
topics: Human resource development as a missing priority
keyPointers: India grew income faster than it grew skill and health
The inadequacy is early childhood, school quality and a usable skill
Measures have to join nutrition, learning and a job, not run three schemes
A demographic bulge without capability is not a dividend

points.text: India treated human beings as a residual of growth rather than as the growth.
Stunting, a weak foundational school and a skill certificate that no employer trusts are the same failure seen at three ages.
The measures are a funded early-years programme, teachers who can teach reading, and apprenticeships tied to a real vacancy rather than to a training target.
HRD is addressed when a child reaches adulthood able to learn a job, not when a ministry reports a number trained.

question_text: Discuss the role of the Competition Commission of India in containing the abuse of dominant position by the Multi-National Corporations in India. Refer to the recent decisions.
topic: CCI and the abuse of dominance by MNCs
topics: CCI and the abuse of dominance by MNCs
keyPointers: Dominance itself is lawful; using it to shut the market is not
MNCs can tie a platform, a price and a data advantage together
CCI can investigate, penalise and order a change of conduct
A fine after the market has tipped is a late remedy

points.text: The Competition Act does not ban a large foreign firm. It bans the use of that size to keep others out.
Predatory pricing, tying an app to a handset, refusing a rival access to a platform, and a deep-discount war funded from abroad are the forms the abuse takes.
CCI has examined such conduct in digital markets, imposed penalties and directed changes in how a platform treats sellers and users.
The role is necessary and slow. Containing an MNC needs a faster interim order, not only a judgment delivered after the rival has died.

question_text: e-governance, as a critical tool of governance, has ushered in effectiveness, transparency and accountability in governments. What inadequacies hamper the enhancement of these features?
topic: What still limits e-governance
topics: What still limits e-governance
keyPointers: A portal does not repair a process that was dishonest offline
Access, language and a failed server exclude the person it was for
Data exist in silos, so the citizen repeats the same proof
Accountability needs a person who answers, not only a tracking number

points.text: E-governance made some services faster and some records public. It did not automatically make government answerable.
Poor connectivity, a single language, low digital skill and a design made for the office rather than the user keep large numbers out.
Departments do not share data, privacy rules are thin, and a grievance portal with no officer behind it is transparency without a remedy.
The inadequacies are last-mile access, joined-up records, and a human who is still responsible when the screen fails.

question_text: ‘Virus of Conflict is affecting the functioning of the SCO’ In the light of the above statement point out the role of India in mitigating the problems.
topic: India and the conflicts inside the SCO
topics: India and the conflicts inside the SCO
keyPointers: The SCO's members include states that are at odds with each other
A regional body cannot function as a bloc while its members are quarrelling
India's role is to keep the body on terror, connectivity and a usable agenda
India will not paper over a bilateral conflict to save a communique

points.text: The Shanghai Cooperation Organisation contains rivalries that its own charter asks members not to import.
Disputes among members, especially over terror and territory, stall statements, joint drills and any claim to be a security provider.
India can narrow the agenda to terrorism, a defined connectivity and a practical economic item, and refuse to let one bilateral fight capture the table.
Mitigation is not mediation of every quarrel. It is keeping the organisation useful for the work all members still share.

question_text: Indian diaspora has scaled new heights in the West. Describe its economic and political benefits for India.
topic: Economic and political benefits of the diaspora in the West
topics: Economic and political benefits of the diaspora in the West
keyPointers: Remittances and investment are the economic return
Skills, technology and a market link are the quieter return
Political benefit is access and a constituency inside the host state
A diaspora is an asset only if India does not treat it as an instrument

points.text: Indians in the West now sit in boardrooms, laboratories and a few cabinets, and India draws on all three.
Remittances, FDI, start-up capital and a demand for Indian goods are the economic benefits.
Politically, an organised diaspora opens doors in Washington, London and elsewhere, and it argues for India inside those systems.
The benefit is real and it is not automatic. It lasts while the relationship is one of respect rather than of extraction.

question_text: “The Constitution of India is a living instrument with capabilities of enormous dynamism. It is a constitution made for a progressive society.” Illustrate with special reference to the expanding horizons of the right to life and personal liberty.
topic: A living Constitution and the expanding right to life
topics: A living Constitution and the expanding right to life
subTopics: Right to life and personal liberty
keyPointers: Article 21 began as a protection against arbitrary loss of life and liberty
The court read procedure, dignity and a set of positive rights into it
Privacy, livelihood, environment and a dignified death arrived by interpretation
Dynamism is legitimate only while it stays inside the text's purpose

points.text: The Constitution was written to be amended and interpreted, not to be frozen in 1950.
Article 21 once meant that life and liberty could be taken by a procedure. After Maneka Gandhi the procedure itself had to be fair, just and reasonable.
From that reading came livelihood, health, a clean environment, legal aid, privacy and dignity, each as a facet of life rather than as a new article.
The expansion tracks a society that asked the court for rights the original list had left unnamed.
The living instrument works when interpretation opens a right the text can bear. It fails when the court starts writing the policy the legislature avoided.

question_text: Explain the constitutional perspectives of Gender Justice with the help of relevant Constitutional Provisions and case laws.
topic: Constitutional perspectives of gender justice
topics: Constitutional perspectives of gender justice
keyPointers: Equality, non-discrimination and special provision sit together
The text allows a difference that corrects a disadvantage
Case law moved the promise into the workplace, the home and the temple
A perspective is not the same as a result

points.text: Gender justice in the Constitution is equality that is allowed to notice inequality.

Articles 14, 15, 16, 39, 42 and 51A forbid discrimination, permit special provision for women, and direct the state toward equal work, a just condition and the renunciation of practices derogatory to women.
Courts have used that text against sexual harassment at work, against a personal law that denied dignity, and for entry and representation that custom had closed.
The perspective treats a formal sameness as insufficient where the starting point was unequal.
The Constitution supplies the standard. Gender justice still depends on a legislature and a local official willing to apply it.

question_text: Account for the legal and political factors responsible for the reduced frequency of using Article 356 by the Union Governments since mid 1990s.
topic: Why Article 356 is used less often
topics: Why Article 356 is used less often
keyPointers: Bommai turned a political weapon into a justiciable power
A floor test replaced the governor's letter as the test
Coalition politics made dismissal expensive
The article remains; the habit of using it did not

points.text: Article 356 was used freely until the court and the party system both made it costly.
S.R. Bommai held that the satisfaction of the President is open to review, that a majority is tested on the floor, and that a mala fide proclamation can be struck down.
Politically, coalition governments at the Centre needed the same regional parties they might have dismissed in the states.
Governors became more cautious, and a dismissal now arrives with a judgment in view.
The fall in frequency is legal restraint plus political arithmetic, not a repeal of the power.

question_text: Discuss the contribution of civil society groups for women's effective and meaningful participation and representation in state legislatures in India.
topic: Civil society and women in state legislatures
topics: Civil society and women in state legislatures
keyPointers: Civil society made the absence of women a public fact
It trained candidates and watched the election
It pushed a reservation that parties would not grant themselves
Representation is meaningful only if the woman is not a proxy

points.text: State legislatures stayed male long after women had the vote, and civil society was one of the forces that refused to treat that as natural.
Groups documented the gap, trained women who had come through panchayats, and campaigned for a reservation in the assemblies.
They also watched whether a selected woman spoke, held a portfolio, or only signed what a male relative decided.
Their contribution is pressure and capacity, not the power to nominate. Parties still choose the ticket.
Civil society made participation thinkable and a proxy harder to hide. The seat itself is still the party's to give.

question_text: Explain the significance of the 101st Constitutional Amendment Act. To what extent does it reflect the accommodative spirit of federalism?
topic: The 101st Amendment and federal accommodation
topics: The 101st Amendment and federal accommodation
keyPointers: The amendment created one tax by asking states to give up several
The Council is the accommodation: a vote, not a diktat
Compensation admitted that the loss would be unequal
The spirit is real and it is strained when rates and dues are imposed

points.text: The 101st Amendment replaced a patchwork of indirect taxes with a goods and services tax that neither Union nor state could run alone.
States gave up sales tax and other levies. The Union gave up exclusive control of the rate. A Council in which states sit together sets the common rules.
A compensation promise recognised that consuming and producing states would lose differently. That is the accommodative part.
Delays in compensation, a dispute over rates and the weight of the Union's vote show the limit of the accommodation.
The amendment is federal in design. It stays accommodative only while the Council behaves like a bargain and not like a Centre.

question_text: Explain the structure of the Parliamentary Committee system. How far have the financial committees helped in the institutionalisation of Indian Parliament?
topic: Parliamentary committees and the financial three
topics: Parliamentary committees and the financial three
keyPointers: Most of Parliament's scrutiny now happens in committee, not on the floor
The financial three examine expenditure, estimates and a public undertaking
They institutionalise a habit of questions the government cannot adjourn
They help only as far as their reports are read and their membership is serious

points.text: The committee system is how a large Parliament examines what the floor has no time to read.
Standing committees on departments, and the three financial committees — Public Accounts, Estimates, and Public Undertakings — divide the work of watching money.
PAC follows the audit, Estimates looks at whether a policy is worth its cost, and the undertakings committee watches public companies. Their reports build a record.
Institutionalisation is the fact that this scrutiny survives a change of government and does not depend on one day's shouting.
The financial committees have helped a great deal, and less than they could, because the House often notes a report and does not act on it.

question_text: “Development and welfare schemes for the vulnerable, by its nature, are discriminatory in approach.” Do you agree? Give reasons for your answer.
topic: Are welfare schemes discriminatory by nature
topics: Are welfare schemes discriminatory by nature
keyPointers: A scheme that selects the vulnerable treats people unequally on purpose
The Constitution calls that a special provision, not a forbidden discrimination
Discrimination in the bad sense is exclusion; here the selection is the remedy
Agreement with the sentence depends on a misuse of the word

points.text: The statement is true only if every unequal treatment is called discrimination. The Constitution does not use the word that way.
A pension for the old, a scholarship for a first-generation student, or a ration for the poorest household leaves others out. That is selection.
Article 15 allows special provision precisely because a formal equality would leave the vulnerable where it found them.
The scheme becomes discriminatory in the bad sense when the criterion is irrelevant, the list is captured, or a person outside the list is punished rather than merely not selected.
Targeted welfare is unequal by design and justified by purpose. Calling all of it discrimination empties a useful word.

question_text: Skill development programmes have succeeded in increasing human resources supply to various sectors. In the context of the statement analyse the linkages between education, skill and employment.
topic: Education, skill and employment
topics: Education, skill and employment
keyPointers: Education builds the person who can be skilled
A skill is usable only if a job is waiting in that form
Supply of trainees is not the same as supply of workers
The missing link is usually the employer, not another course

points.text: A skill certificate increases a number. It increases employment only if education, the skill and a vacancy are the same pipeline.
Schooling that does not teach reading and number cannot be repaired by a short course at eighteen.
A skill designed without an employer produces a trained person the sector does not hire, which is a supply only on paper.
Apprenticeship, a local industry setting the syllabus, and a placement that is counted are the actual linkages.
Programmes have raised supply in the sense of enrolment. The linkage to employment is still the weak joint.

question_text: ‘The expansion and strengthening of NATO and a stronger US-Europe strategic partnership works well for India.’ What is your opinion about this statement? Give reasons and examples to support your answer.
topic: NATO's strengthening and India's interest
topics: NATO's strengthening and India's interest
keyPointers: A stronger Europe that balances Russia and China can suit India
It also hardens a world of blocs India has tried not to join
The test is whether the partnership leaves India room with Russia and in the Indo-Pacific
It works well only up to the point where India is asked to choose

points.text: The statement is partly right. A capable Europe is useful to India, and a closed Western bloc is not.
NATO's renewal after Ukraine checks a revisionist Russia and keeps the United States tied to a rules-based order India also invokes against coercion in Asia.
The same renewal polarises forums, complicates India's defence ties with Russia, and can drag every issue into a camp.
India gains from European investment, technology and a second partner in the Indo-Pacific, as in its closer ties with France and the EU.
It works well when it adds partners. It works badly when it demands that India treat the world as already divided.

question_text: ‘Sea is an important Component of the Cosmos’ Discuss in the light of the above statement the role of the IMO (International Maritime Organisation) in protecting environment and enhancing maritime safety and security.
topic: The IMO, the sea, safety and the environment
topics: The IMO, the sea, safety and the environment
keyPointers: The sea is a shared highway and a shared ecology
IMO writes the rules of the ship because no one state owns the lane
Safety, security and pollution are three uses of the same rulebook
A convention protects the sea only when flag states enforce it

points.text: If the sea is a component of a single world, then the ship on it cannot be left to the law of whichever flag is cheapest.
The IMO sets standards for the safety of life at sea, for seafarers, and for how a ship is built and run.
On the environment it regulates oil, garbage, ballast water and the carbon of shipping. On security it sets rules against piracy, a stowaway threat and an unlawful act at sea.
India, as a large coastline and a growing fleet, is both a maker and a subject of these rules.
The IMO's role is to make one ship's negligence everyone else's business, and then to make that business enforceable.
